slides.heading: Forms of Business Organisation
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **sole proprietorship**, the **Joint Hindu Family business** and the **partnership**.

slides.narration: A baker opening a small shop, a family running a spice trade and three friends starting a consultancy all need to decide how to organise their business. In this part we study three forms: the sole proprietorship, the Joint Hindu Family business and the partnership, and see who bears the risk in each.

slides.heading: The forms at a glance

bullets: One owner: sole proprietorship
A family: Joint Hindu Family business
Two or more persons: partnership
Members with a common need: cooperative society
Shareholders: company

slides.narration: The form of organisation decides who owns the business, who takes the risk and how long it lasts. The tree shows five main forms. In this part we look at the first three. The cooperative society and the company, with its private, public and one person kinds, come in the next part.

slides.heading: Sole proprietorship
slides.body_md: A **sole proprietorship** is a business owned, managed and controlled by one person, who receives all the profit and bears all the risk.

rows: Owned, managed and controlled by one person
Personal property can pay business debts
All profit and all loss belong to the owner
Owner and business are one in law
The life of the business depends on the owner

visual.alt: Table of six features of a sole proprietorship: one owner, unlimited liability, sole risk bearer, no separate entity, easy formation and closure, and lack of continuity

slides.narration: A sole proprietorship is a business owned, managed and controlled by one person. That person receives all the profit and bears all the risk. The owner and the business are one in law, so there is no separate legal entity, and the owner has unlimited liability. It is easy to start and to close, but it usually ends with the owner.

slides.heading: Merits and limitations of a sole proprietorship
bullets: Quick decisions and full control
Confidentiality and direct incentive
But resources, life and skills are limited

visual.alt: Table of the merits and limitations of a sole proprietorship

slides.narration: The strengths are quick decisions, confidentiality, a direct reward for effort, a sense of accomplishment and easy formation and closure. The weaknesses are limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability and limited managerial ability, because one person cannot be an expert in everything.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: unlimited liability
slides.body_md: An imagined shop owes more than its assets are worth.
bullets: Step 1: Find the debt and the assets.
Step 2: Subtract to find the shortfall.
Step 3: Decide who pays. Owner and business are one, so the owner does.

rows: Owed to creditors by an imagined shop
Assets of the shop that can be sold

visual.alt: Worked example table: an imagined shop owes the shortfall between debts and assets, which the sole proprietor must pay from personal property because liability is unlimited
visual.caption: Imagined figures. Subtract assets from debts.

slides.narration: Take an imagined shop whose debts are larger than its assets. Subtract the assets from the debts to get the shortfall. Because a sole proprietor and the business are one in law, the shortfall is recovered from the owner, even if it means selling the owner home or savings. This is what unlimited liability means.

slides.heading: Quick check: a merit of the form
slides.body_md: Identify the merit shown in an imagined tailor shop.
slides.narration: Read the case carefully and ask which strength of the sole proprietorship it shows. Think about who decides, and how fast.

slides.heading: Joint Hindu Family business
slides.body_md: A **Joint Hindu Family business** is owned and carried on by the members of a Hindu Undivided Family and is governed by Hindu law.

rows: Members of a Hindu Undivided Family
Hindu law, not by an agreement
Mitakshara in most of India; Dayabhaga in West Bengal (as commonly taught)

visual.alt: Table of the Joint Hindu Family business: owned by a Hindu Undivided Family, governed by Hindu law, membership by birth, managed by the Karta, with the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga systems as commonly taught

slides.narration: A Joint Hindu Family business is owned and carried on by the members of a Hindu Undivided Family, and it is governed by Hindu law. The eldest member, called the Karta, manages it. Members are called coparceners and join by birth. As commonly taught, the Mitakshara system applies in most of India and the Dayabhaga system in West Bengal.

slides.heading: Liability, continuity and a dated note
bullets: The Karta has unlimited liability.
Coparceners are liable only up to their share.
The business goes on after the Karta dies.
As of 2024, daughters are coparceners by birth, as per the Hindu Succession Amendment Act of 2005.

nodes.label: Coparceners: liability limited to their share
Business continues after the Karta dies

visual.alt: Flow showing the Karta with unlimited liability, coparceners with liability limited to their share, and the business continuing after the death of the Karta

slides.narration: The Karta has unlimited liability, but the coparceners are liable only up to their share in the business. If the Karta dies, the business goes on and the next senior member takes charge. Note the date: since the Hindu Succession Amendment Act of two thousand five, daughters are coparceners by birth, as of two thousand twenty four.

slides.heading: Merits and limitations of the family business
bullets: Strengths: control, continuity, secrecy
Weaknesses: capital, Karta unlimited, dominance

visual.alt: Table of merits and limitations of the Joint Hindu Family business

slides.narration: The family business has strong control under the Karta, continuity after his death, limited liability for coparceners and secrecy within the family. Its limits are small capital, the unlimited liability of the Karta, the risk that one strong Karta dominates others, and a shortage of managerial skills outside the family.

slides.heading: Quick check: continuity
slides.body_md: True or false: what happens when the Karta dies?
slides.narration: Think about whether the business depends on one person, or on the family as a whole.

slides.heading: Partnership: meaning and features
slides.body_md: A **partnership** is the relationship between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all, or by any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act 1932).

rows: Affected by retirement, death or insolvency
Each partner is agent and principal

visual.alt: Table of seven features of a partnership: formation by agreement, unlimited liability, risk bearing, shared control, continuity, number of members and mutual agency

slides.narration: The Indian Partnership Act of nineteen thirty two sees a partnership as a relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all of them, or by any of them acting for all. It begins with an agreement, liability is unlimited, and there must be at least two partners and, as of two thousand twenty four, no more than fifty.

slides.heading: Mutual agency
slides.body_md: Each partner is both an **agent** and a **principal**. An act of one partner within the business of the firm binds the others.

nodes.label: Partner A acts for the firm
Acts as agent of B and C

visual.alt: Flow of mutual agency: an act by partner A for the firm is an act as agent of B and C, so they are bound

slides.narration: In a partnership, each partner is an agent of the others and also a principal. So when one partner makes a contract for the firm, within the scope of its business, the other partners are bound by it. This feature is called mutual agency, and it is why partners must trust one another.

slides.narration: Partners differ in what they do and what others know. An active partner works in the firm. A sleeping partner invests but does not manage. A secret partner manages, but the public does not know. A nominal partner only lends a name. A partner by estoppel or by holding out is liable because of conduct. A minor is admitted to the benefits only.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sharing profit and facing debt
slides.body_md: An imagined advisory firm earns a profit, and later owes more than it owns.
bullets: Step 1: Add the ratio parts.
Step 2: Divide the profit by the total, then multiply by each part.
Step 3: Debt: joint and several liability lets a creditor claim the whole from any one partner.

visual.alt: Worked example table: a profit of four lakh eighty thousand rupees shared in the ratio three, two and one gives two lakh forty thousand, one lakh sixty thousand and eighty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Profit of Rs 4,80,000, divided into 6 equal parts.

slides.narration: Here the profit is shared in the ratio three, two and one. Add the parts to get six. Divide the profit by six and multiply by each part of each partner. If the firm later owes more than it owns, joint and several liability means a creditor may claim the whole shortfall from any one partner, who must then recover the rest from the others.

slides.heading: Joint and several liability
bullets: Joint: all partners are liable together.
Several: each is liable for the whole, separately.

rows: Creditor may claim the whole shortfall from

visual.alt: Table: a firm owing six lakh rupees with assets of three lakh eighty thousand has a shortfall of two lakh twenty thousand, which the creditor may claim in full from any one partner because liability is joint and several
visual.caption: Joint and several: each partner can be asked to pay the whole.

slides.narration: Look at this imagined firm. Its debts are larger than its assets, so there is a shortfall. Because the liability of partners is joint and several, a creditor may claim the whole shortfall from any single partner, even a partner who holds a small share. Such a partner can then claim a contribution from the others.

slides.heading: Types of partnership and the deed
slides.body_md: A **partnership deed** is the written agreement among the partners. A **limited liability partnership**, governed by the LLP Act 2008, is a separate kind with limited liability.

rows: Partnership at will; partnership for a particular venture
General partnership; limited liability partnership (LLP Act 2008)

visual.alt: Table of types of partnership by duration and by liability

slides.narration: By duration, a partnership may be at will, with no fixed period, or for a particular venture. By liability, it may be a general partnership, with unlimited liability, or a limited liability partnership, which is governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act of two thousand eight and gives its partners limited liability.

slides.heading: Contents of a partnership deed
bullets: A written deed avoids disputes
It is a good practice, not a legal necessity

rows: Name of the firm and nature of business

visual.alt: Table of what a partnership deed usually contains and why: name and nature of business, capital, profit-sharing ratio, salaries and interest, and admission and retirement rules

slides.narration: A partnership deed is a written agreement. It usually states the name of the firm, the nature of the business, the capital of each partner, the profit sharing ratio, salaries and interest, and the rules for admitting and retiring partners. Putting these in writing prevents later quarrels.

slides.heading: Registration of a partnership
bullets: Registration is optional.
Without it, the right to sue is limited, as of 2024.

headers: If the firm is not registered (as of 2024)
rows: Cannot sue to enforce contract rights
Cannot sue to enforce deed rights

visual.alt: Table of consequences of not registering a partnership as of 2024: the firm cannot sue third parties and a partner cannot sue the firm or other partners, although registration is optional

slides.narration: Registering a partnership is optional. But as of two thousand twenty four, an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce its contract rights, and a partner cannot sue the firm or the other partners to enforce rights under the deed. For this reason most firms choose to register.

slides.narration: To sum up. A sole proprietorship has one owner, unlimited liability and limited resources. In a Joint Hindu Family business the Karta manages, and only the Karta has unlimited liability. A partnership rests on an agreement, with unlimited joint and several liability and mutual agency. Remember the seven types of partners and the optional registration.

bullets: Add as of 2024 to every legal figure.
Link each concept to the case in the question.

rows: Writing that coparceners have unlimited liability
It is optional; the penalty is loss of the right to sue
Secret: manages but unknown. Sleeping: known but inactive

visual.alt: Exam tips table: four common mistakes about the Joint Hindu Family business, partnership registration, types of partners and dated legal limits

slides.narration: Some tips. Only the Karta has unlimited liability, not the coparceners. Registration of a partnership is optional. Do not confuse a secret partner with a sleeping partner. And whenever you write a number fixed by law, such as fifty partners, add the words as of two thousand twenty four.

slides.heading: Cooperatives, Companies and Choice
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **cooperative society**, the **company**, and how to **choose** a form.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: cooperative society, company, private and public company, stages of formation, and choosing a form
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Thirty dairy farmers who sell milk together and a factory that needs huge funds are very different businesses. In this part we study the cooperative society, the company with its private and public kinds, the stages in forming a company, and how to choose the right form for a given case.

slides.heading: Cooperative society: features
slides.body_md: A **cooperative society** is a voluntary association of persons who join together for the welfare of the members.

rows: Registered: Cooperative Societies Act 1912 or a state law

visual.alt: Table of five features of a cooperative society: voluntary membership, legal status, limited liability, democratic control and service motive

slides.narration: A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons who join together for the welfare of the members. It is registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of nineteen twelve or a state law. Members can join or leave freely, their liability is limited, each has one vote, and the aim is service rather than profit alone.

slides.heading: Types of cooperatives
bullets: Six types: consumer, producer, marketing, farmer, credit and housing.

rows: Buys goods in bulk for members at fair prices
Supplies raw materials and tools to small producers
Helps farmers with inputs, equipment and sale
Lends to members from pooled savings
Builds or buys homes for members

visual.alt: Table of six types of cooperatives: consumer, producer, marketing, farmer, credit and housing

slides.narration: There are six types. A consumer cooperative buys for its members. A producer cooperative supplies inputs to small producers. A marketing cooperative sells the products of the members together. A farmer cooperative helps farmers with inputs and sale. A credit cooperative lends from pooled savings, and a housing society builds homes.

sections.heading: 1. Sole proprietorship
sections.body_md:
A one-person business in which the owner decides, receives every rupee of profit and bears every loss.

**Features:** easy formation and closure with few formalities; unlimited liability; sole risk bearer and profit recipient; full control; no separate legal entity; lack of continuity.

**Merits:** quick decisions, confidentiality, direct incentive, sense of accomplishment, ease of formation and closure.

**Limitations:** limited resources, limited life, unlimited liability, limited managerial ability.

key_terms.definition_md: A business owned, managed and controlled by one person who receives all profit and bears all risk.
Responsibility for debts that extends to the owner's personal property.

sections.heading: 2. Joint Hindu Family business
sections.body_md:
Run by members of a Hindu Undivided Family and governed by Hindu law. Membership comes by birth; members are **coparceners**. The eldest member, the **Karta**, manages it.

**Systems (as commonly taught):** Mitakshara in most of India; Dayabhaga in West Bengal.

**Liability:** unlimited for the Karta; limited to their share for coparceners. The business continues after the Karta's death.

**Dated note:** daughters became coparceners by birth through the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005, so as of 2024 they hold the same position as sons.

**Merits and limitations:** see the table.

key_terms.definition_md: The eldest member who manages a Joint Hindu Family business.
A member of the family who joins the business by birth and has a share in it.

sections.heading: 3. Partnership
sections.body_md:
The relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business carried on by all of them or by any acting for all (Indian Partnership Act 1932).

**Features:** formation by agreement; unlimited liability, joint and several; risk bearing; shared decisions and control; limited continuity; minimum 2 and maximum 50 members as of 2024 under company law rules; mutual agency.

**Partnership deed:** a written agreement; usually states name, nature of business, capital, profit-sharing ratio, salaries and interest, and the rules for admission and retirement.

**Registration** is optional, but as of 2024 an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce contracts, and partners cannot sue the firm or each other to enforce deed rights.

key_terms.definition_md: A relationship between persons who agree to share the profits of a business run by all or any of them for all.
The feature under which every partner is both an agent and a principal of the firm.
Each partner is liable together with the others and also separately for the whole of the firm's debts.

rows: Affected by retirement, death or insolvency
Each partner is agent and principal

sections.heading: 4. Types of partners and partnerships
sections.body_md:
**Partners:** active (works), sleeping (invests, does not manage), secret (manages, unknown to public), nominal (lends only a name), partner by estoppel (liable through misleading conduct), partner by holding out (held out as a partner and does not deny it), minor (admitted to the benefits only).

**Partnerships by duration:** at will; for a particular venture. **By liability:** general partnership; limited liability partnership, governed by the LLP Act 2008, with a separate legal identity and limited liability of partners.

key_terms.definition_md: A partner who contributes capital and shares profit but takes no active part in management.
A person who is not a partner but becomes liable because his own conduct led others to believe he was one.

sections.heading: 5. Cooperative society
sections.body_md:
A voluntary association of persons joined for the welfare of members, registered under the Cooperative Societies Act 1912 or a state law.

**Features:** voluntary membership; legal status through registration; limited liability; democratic control (one member, one vote); service motive.

**Types:** consumer's, producer's, marketing, farmer's, credit, housing.

**Merits:** equal voting, limited liability, stable existence, economy, ease of formation. **Limitations:** limited funds, inefficient management, red tape, lack of secrecy, government control.

key_terms.definition_md: A voluntary association of persons who join to serve the welfare of the members.

rows: Buys goods in bulk for members at fair prices
Supplies raw materials and tools to small producers
Helps farmers with inputs, equipment and sale
Lends to members from pooled savings
Builds or buys homes for members

sections.heading: 6. Company and the choice of form
sections.body_md:
An association of persons incorporated under the Companies Act 2013, with separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability. **Features:** artificial person, formation by registration, board of directors, risk borne by shareholders, common seal optional since 2015 (as of 2024).

**Private company:** 2 to 200 members (as of 2024, excluding employees); restricts transfer; cannot invite the public; min 2 directors; name ends Private Limited. **Public company:** min 7 members, no maximum; free transfer; can invite the public; min 3 directors. A One Person Company was introduced by the 2013 Act.

**Stages:** promotion, incorporation, capital subscription (public company), commencement; as of 2024 a declaration is filed (introduced 2019), where older books say certificate of commencement.

**Choice:** weigh cost and ease, liability, continuity, management ability, capital, control and nature of business.

key_terms.definition_md: An association of persons incorporated under company law, with a legal entity of its own, perpetual succession and limited liability.
Continuing existence of the company regardless of changes in its members.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that coparceners have unlimited liability; only the Karta does.
- Calling registration of a partnership compulsory.
- Giving 50 partners, 200 members or the declaration on commencement without the words as of 2024.
- Choosing a form without tying it to two or more factors.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a correct option or a quoted line from the case.
- 2 and 3 marks: one point per feature or merit with a short explanation.
- 5 marks: five points, each with an explanation, in a numbered list.
- Case questions: quote the line, name the concept, explain in a sentence.

cards.front_md: Seven factors in choosing a form
cards.back_md: Cost and ease, liability, continuity, management ability, capital, control, nature of business.

questions.stem_md: Chandrika Naik runs Naik Bakes, an imagined bakery in the imagined town of Chandpur, entirely on her own. Her creditors are owed Rs 2,40,000, but the shop's assets can raise only Rs 1,50,000. The unpaid Rs 90,000 can be recovered from

options.text_md: only the bakery's assets, because her liability is limited to the business
Chandrika's personal property, because a sole proprietor has unlimited liability
her customers, who must share the loss
nobody, because a sole proprietorship is a separate legal entity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Chandrika's personal property, because a sole proprietor has unlimited liability. The owner and the business are one in law, so there is no ring-fence around personal assets. Limited liability belongs to companies and cooperatives; customers never share a trader's loss; and a sole proprietorship has no separate legal existence.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following does NOT describe a sole proprietorship?

options.text_md: One person bears all the risk and keeps all the profit
It can be started and wound up with few legal formalities
The business has no separate legal identity from its owner
The owner's liability for business debts is limited to the capital put in

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The owner's liability for business debts is limited to the capital put in. Liability of a sole proprietor is unlimited, so the first statement is the one that does not fit. The other three are standard features: single risk bearer, simple formation and closure, and no separate legal entity.

questions.stem_md: Gopal Rane, an imagined tailor in an imagined suburb, decides on a new blouse design on Monday and starts stitching it on Tuesday, since he does not have to consult anyone. Which merit of a sole proprietorship does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Quick decision making. One person decides, so there is no delay in consultation. Large capital, perpetual succession and limited liability are not merits of this form; its resources are small, its life is tied to the owner and its liability is unlimited.

questions.stem_md: Aarav Tiwari, who owns an imagined cycle-repair workshop in an imagined town, cannot buy a second compressor because his own savings and one small loan are all he can raise. This points to which limitation of a sole proprietorship?

options.text_md: Lack of any control over the business
Heavy legal formalities for closing the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Limited resources. A sole proprietor depends on personal savings and borrowing, so growth is held back by limited resources. He has full control, the form ends with the owner rather than lasting forever, and closing it is easy.

questions.stem_md: A person becomes a member (coparcener) of a Joint Hindu Family business

options.text_md: by signing an agreement with the Karta
by paying a share of the capital
by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family
by registering with the Registrar of Companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** by birth in the Hindu Undivided Family. Membership of this form arises by birth in the family, not by contract, purchase of shares or registration, which is why the form is governed by Hindu law rather than by an agreement.

questions.stem_md: In Bhatia and Sons, an imagined Joint Hindu Family business of Indore, Karta Mohan runs the shop while his brothers and nephews are coparceners. Which statement about liability is correct?

options.text_md: Mohan's liability is unlimited, while each coparcener is liable only up to his or her share in the business
Mohan's liability is limited, while the coparceners have unlimited liability
Every member's liability is limited to the salary drawn

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Mohan's liability is unlimited, while each coparcener is liable only up to his or her share in the business. The Karta, who manages and takes decisions, bears unlimited liability; the other members are liable only to the extent of their share. The other options reverse or flatten this arrangement.

questions.stem_md: As commonly taught, the Dayabhaga system of Hindu law, under which a Joint Hindu Family business may be governed, is followed mainly in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** West Bengal. Dayabhaga is the system associated with West Bengal; the rest of India follows the Mitakshara system.

questions.stem_md: Karta Raghunath of Raghunath Brothers Oils, an imagined family firm of Rajkot, passed away. Which outcome fits the Joint Hindu Family form?

options.text_md: The business ends automatically on his death
The business carries on, and the next senior member takes charge as Karta
The business becomes a company with immediate effect
Creditors may force closure within a month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The business carries on, and the next senior member takes charge as Karta. Because the form rests on the family and not on one person, the death of the Karta does not end the business; the eldest remaining member steps up. Automatic dissolution would apply to forms whose life depends on one person.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, after the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005, a daughter in a Hindu Undivided Family

options.text_md: becomes a coparcener by birth, like a son
becomes a coparcener only on marriage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** becomes a coparcener by birth, like a son. The 2005 amendment gave daughters the same right as sons to be coparceners by birth. It did not require marriage or an automatic appointment as Karta.

questions.stem_md: Hari Bhat put Rs 4,00,000 into Lakshmi Sweets, an imagined partnership firm, and joins in its decisions, but the firm's customers and suppliers do not know he is a partner. Hari is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** secret partner. A secret partner shares in management and profit while his link with the firm stays hidden from the public. A sleeping partner is known but inactive; a nominal partner only lends a name; a partner by estoppel is bound by his own misleading conduct.

questions.stem_md: Pradeep is not a partner in Gill and Rao Traders, an imagined firm. At a bank meeting he spoke and acted as if he were one, and the officer lent money to the firm on that belief. Pradeep can be held liable as a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** partner by estoppel. He is bound by his own conduct, which led the lender to believe he was a partner. He did not invest or work in the firm, so he is neither sleeping nor active, and nothing suggests he is a minor.

questions.stem_md: Sana and Ritu run an unregistered partnership firm in imagined Nashik. A customer refuses to pay for goods supplied. As of 2024, what is the legal position?

options.text_md: The firm can sue freely, since registration matters only for companies
The firm is illegal and must be closed at once
The customer is released from the debt
The firm cannot sue the customer to enforce the contract, because it is not registered

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The firm cannot sue the customer to enforce the contract, because it is not registered. Registration of a partnership is optional, but an unregistered firm loses the right to file such a suit against third parties. It is not illegal, and the debt is not wiped out.

questions.stem_md: Sixty traders of an imagined market town want to run one grain business as a single partnership firm. As of 2024, why can they not do so?

options.text_md: A partnership needs at least 100 members
Partnership is not allowed for trading activities
Only a company may have more than two members
The maximum number of partners prescribed under company law rules is 50

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The maximum number of partners prescribed under company law rules is 50. Under the rules made under the Companies Act 2013, an ordinary partnership may have at most 50 partners as of 2024. The minimum is two, trading is allowed, and a company is not the only form with many members.

questions.stem_md: Dr Isha Menon invests in an imagined clinic-supplies partnership and shares its profit, but never takes part in running it, and everyone knows she is a partner. She is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** sleeping partner. Investing and sharing profit without working in the firm, openly, is the mark of a sleeping (dormant) partner. A secret partner is unknown to the public, an active partner works, and a nominal partner contributes nothing but a name.

questions.stem_md: Nisha and Tarun start an imagined catering firm with no fixed period and no single venture in view, and either may end it by giving notice. Their firm is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** partnership at will. With no fixed period or venture and a right to leave on notice, it is a partnership at will. A venture partnership ends when its single task ends; the other two forms are governed by different laws.

questions.stem_md: Which item would NOT normally be written in a partnership deed?

options.text_md: A prospectus inviting the public to invest in the firm
The ratio in which profits and losses are shared
Interest on capital and salaries of working partners
Rules for admitting and retiring partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A prospectus inviting the public to invest in the firm. A firm cannot invite the public to invest, so a prospectus has no place in the deed. The profit-sharing ratio, interest and salaries, and rules on admission and retirement are all standard clauses.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a limited liability partnership formed under the LLP Act 2008 is correct?

options.text_md: It has no legal identity apart from its partners
It is a separate legal entity, and its partners are not personally liable for its debts beyond their agreed contribution
All its partners always have unlimited liability
It may invite the public to buy its shares

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is a separate legal entity, and its partners are not personally liable for its debts beyond their agreed contribution. The LLP blends the flexibility of a partnership with limited liability and a separate identity. It is not an unlimited-liability firm and, being a partnership, does not raise money by issuing shares to the public.

questions.stem_md: Fifty orange growers of imagined Sundarpur pool their harvest and sell it together through one society to bargain for a better price with city buyers. This is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** marketing cooperative. Joint selling to get a better price is the job of a marketing cooperative. A consumer's cooperative buys for its members, a housing society builds homes, and a credit cooperative lends money.

questions.stem_md: At the general meeting of an imagined weavers' society, a member holding many shares and a member holding one share each cast a single vote. Which feature of a cooperative is shown?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Democratic control. One member, one vote, whatever the shareholding, is democratic control. Service motive concerns the aim, limited liability concerns debts, and legal status concerns registration.

questions.stem_md: Orchid Packaging Limited, an imagined company, signed a supply contract in its own name and later sued a buyer who failed to pay. Its largest shareholder, Mr Das, was not a party to the suit. This is possible because a company

options.text_md: is the same person as its largest shareholder
can act only through a partnership deed
is a separate legal entity that can sue and be sued in its own name
has unlimited liability, so its owners may sue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** is a separate legal entity that can sue and be sued in its own name. Incorporation creates a legal person distinct from its members, so the company itself sues. It is not identical to its shareholder, no partnership deed is involved, and its liability is limited, not unlimited.

questions.stem_md: Which set of figures gives the minimum number of members and directors of a private company, as of 2024?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 2 members and 2 directors. A private company needs at least 2 members and 2 directors; the 7 and 3 are the minimums for a public company.

questions.stem_md: Kesari Hospitality Private Limited, an imagined company, was incorporated last month and will never ask the public to buy its shares. Which stage of formation does it leave out?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Capital subscription. Capital subscription is the stage in which a public company invites the public to apply for shares. A private company may not do this, so it skips that stage but still goes through promotion, incorporation and the commencement step.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, how does company law treat the common seal?

options.text_md: It is compulsory for every company
It is allowed only for public companies
It is prohibited for all companies
It is optional, since an amendment of 2015

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It is optional, since an amendment of 2015. The 2015 amendment made the common seal optional for companies, so it is neither compulsory nor banned, and it is not limited to public companies.

questions.stem_md: A One Person Company, a form introduced by the Companies Act 2013, has

options.text_md: a single member and a separate legal entity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a single member and a separate legal entity. The form lets one individual run a company with limited liability and a legal identity of its own. It must have one member, so zero members or seven members are wrong, and liability is limited.

questions.stem_md: Before registering Tamarind Foods Limited, an imagined company, its founders judged whether demand would justify a plant, chose a name and hired professionals to prepare the documents. This is the stage of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** promotion. Conceiving the idea, studying its feasibility, selecting a name and preparing documents are the work of promotion. Incorporation is registration itself, and the other two stages come later.

questions.stem_md: Vindhya Steel Works, an imagined firm, plans a plant needing several hundred crore rupees of capital, and its promoters want it to last beyond their own lives and to draw in many investors. The most suitable form is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a public company. Large capital, continuity and a wide base of investors point to a public company. The other forms are limited in capital, in continuity or in the number of people who can contribute.

questions.stem_md: Forty dairy farmers of imagined Gokulpur, each with a few cows, want to sell milk jointly, share a chilling plant and keep middlemen out, with an equal say regardless of herd size. The most suitable form is

options.text_md: a public company that issues a prospectus

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a cooperative society. Joint effort, mutual welfare and equal voting match a cooperative society. A sole proprietorship or a One Person Company has just one owner, and a public company would give votes by shareholding and impose heavy formalities.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A sole proprietor's personal property can be used to pay the debts of the business.

**Reason (R):** A sole proprietorship has no separate legal existence apart from its owner.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Since the law treats owner and business as one, creditors can reach the owner's own property, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A company can hold property in its own name.

**Reason (R):** A shareholder's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on the shares held.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. Holding property follows from separate legal existence, whereas limited liability concerns what a member must pay for company debts; the second statement does not explain the first.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An act of one partner within the scope of the firm's business can bind all the other partners.

**Reason (R):** Every partner is both an agent and a principal in relation to the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because each partner acts as agent for the others and is also their principal, one partner's authorised act binds the rest; R is the reason (mutual agency).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A cooperative society works mainly for the welfare of its members.

**Reason (R):** Members of a cooperative society always share its entire surplus equally, whatever their contribution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: service to members is the aim. R is false: surplus is shared on rules such as business done with the society, and part is kept in reserves, so it is not always divided equally.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The shares of a public company are freely transferable.

**Reason (R):** A public company cannot have more than 200 members.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the cap of 200 (as of 2024) applies to a private company; a public company has no maximum number of members.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every member of a Joint Hindu Family business has unlimited liability.

**Reason (R):** The liability of the coparceners is limited to their share in the business.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false, because only the Karta has unlimited liability. R is true, as coparceners answer only to the extent of their share.

questions.stem_md: A Joint Hindu Family business carries on even after the death of its Karta.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The business rests on the family, not on one person, so the next senior member takes charge.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, the law says an imagined partnership firm in Surat must be registered before it may begin business.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Registration of a partnership is optional; it only affects the firm's ability to sue, and the firm may legally begin work without it.

questions.stem_md: In a cooperative society, a member who buys more shares gets more votes at the general meeting.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Every member has one vote irrespective of shareholding; this is democratic control.

questions.stem_md: A private company is not allowed to invite the public to subscribe to its shares.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Only a public company may approach the public for capital; this is one of the restrictions on a private company.

questions.stem_md: A partnership needs a minimum of ___ persons, and as of 2024 the maximum number of partners is ___.
questions.solution_md: The minimum is 2 persons and the maximum is 50 partners as of 2024.

questions.stem_md: The name of a private company ends with the words ___, whereas the name of a public company ends with the word ___.
questions.solution_md: Private Limited for a private company, and Limited for a public company.

questions.stem_md: In a Joint Hindu Family business the ___ manages the business, and the other members are called ___.
questions.solution_md: The Karta manages; the others are coparceners.

questions.stem_md: Match each description of a partner in an imagined firm with the type of partner.

options.text_md: Works in the firm and takes part in its day-to-day running
Puts in capital and shares profit but does not manage
Lends only his name to the firm, with no capital or work
Becomes liable because his own conduct misled others

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each type is defined by role in management and by what the outside world knows or is led to believe.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined group with the type of cooperative it forms.

options.text_md: Families of an apartment block pool money to buy land and build flats
Students of an imagined college jointly run a shop selling stationery at fair prices
Small potters pool the cost of clay and kilns for their own production
Villagers lend each other small sums out of their joint savings

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Housing for members, buying for members, helping small producers produce, and lending to members are the four different purposes.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature with the form of business organisation it best describes.

options.text_md: Manager holds authority and members answer only up to their share
Owners act as agents of one another
May invite the public and has no maximum number of members

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The Karta structure, mutual agency, the public invitation without a cap on members, and equal voting each identify one form.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages in forming a public company in the order they happen.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Ideas and documents come first, registration next, then raising capital from the public, and finally the declaration that allows business to start.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these promotion activities of an imagined company in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Choose and get approval for a name

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (b) → (d). A promoter first finds an idea, tests it, then secures a name and finally prepares the paperwork.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Who is the Karta of a Joint Hindu Family business, and what is his liability?
questions.solution_md: One mark for the role of the Karta and one for the liability contrast.

answer.model_answer_md: The Karta is the eldest member of the family, who manages the business and takes decisions on behalf of the family. His liability is unlimited, whereas the other members, the coparceners, are liable only up to their share in the business.

marking_scheme.step: Karta is the eldest member who manages
Karta unlimited; coparceners limited to share

questions.stem_md: Define a cooperative society and name the law under which it is registered.
questions.solution_md: Definition with welfare motive, and the registering law.

answer.model_answer_md: A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons who join together for the welfare of its members rather than for profit as such. It is registered under the Cooperative Societies Act 1912 or the cooperative law of a state, as of 2024.

marking_scheme.step: Registered under the 1912 Act or state law

questions.stem_md: Neha Pillai, an imagined former clerk, starts a home-baking business alone. State two merits of this form that she will enjoy.
questions.solution_md: Any two merits, each linked to Neha.

answer.model_answer_md: First, she can take quick decisions without consulting anyone, so she can change a recipe or price at once. Second, she keeps all the profit, which gives her a direct incentive to work hard, and she can start or close the venture with very few formalities.

questions.stem_md: State two restrictions that apply to a private company but not to a public company.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the three restrictions.

answer.model_answer_md: A private company must restrict the right to transfer its shares, and it cannot invite the public to subscribe to its shares. It is also limited to a maximum of 200 members, excluding employees, as of 2024, while a public company has no such limit.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a sleeping partner and a nominal partner.
questions.solution_md: Contrast the two on capital, profit and management.

answer.model_answer_md: A sleeping partner invests capital and shares in the profit but takes no active part in management. A nominal partner contributes no capital and gets no share of profit; he only allows the firm to use his name, though he remains liable to outsiders.

marking_scheme.step: Sleeping partner described with capital and profit
Nominal partner described as lending only a name

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, is a common seal compulsory for a company? State the position and the year of the change.
questions.solution_md: Optional, since 2015.

answer.model_answer_md: No. A common seal is optional for a company, a change made by an amendment to the Companies Act in 2015. A company may still have one, but documents can also be authenticated by authorised signatories.

questions.stem_md: Why might three consultants, who want to start an imagined advisory firm, prefer a limited liability partnership to an ordinary partnership? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Limited liability and separate legal entity or continuity.

answer.model_answer_md: In a limited liability partnership under the LLP Act 2008, the partners are not personally liable for the firm's debts beyond their agreed contribution, so their homes are safer. The firm is also a separate legal entity with continuity, unlike an ordinary partnership.

questions.stem_md: What is a One Person Company, and which Act introduced it?
questions.solution_md: Single member with limited liability; Companies Act 2013.

answer.model_answer_md: A One Person Company is a company with a single member, so one individual can run a business with limited liability and a legal existence separate from his own. It was introduced by the Companies Act 2013.

questions.stem_md: Explain mutual agency with an example from an imagined firm, Rao and Bose Timber, run by two partners.
questions.solution_md: Agent and principal, with the example.

answer.model_answer_md: Each partner is an agent of the others as well as a principal. So if Rao buys timber for the firm within the scope of its business, Bose is bound by that purchase as if he had made it himself, and the firm's assets and both partners answer for it.

marking_scheme.step: Each partner is both agent and principal

questions.stem_md: A sole proprietor's business is said to lack continuity. Explain this in two points with an imagined example, a stationery shop in Lucknow.
questions.solution_md: Business ends or is disrupted with the owner's illness or death.

answer.model_answer_md: The shop and the owner are one in law, so if the owner falls seriously ill, becomes bankrupt or dies, the business may stop. Continuing it after her needs a fresh start by a successor, who must restart with new licences and customers.

marking_scheme.step: Business and owner not separate, so life depends on owner

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, what must a company that has share capital do before it starts business, and since when?
questions.solution_md: Declaration before commencing; introduced 2019.

answer.model_answer_md: As of 2024, it files a declaration with the Registrar confirming that the subscribers have paid for the shares they agreed to take. This requirement was introduced in 2019; older books speak of a certificate of commencement.

questions.stem_md: Gita, Imran and Sumeet, three friends, are about to open an imagined tuition firm. List three items they should put into their partnership deed, with one line on each.

answer.model_answer_md: First, the profit-sharing ratio, so that nobody disputes who gets what. Second, the capital each will bring and the interest on it, which fixes their stakes. Third, rules for admitting a new partner and for retirement, which lets the firm carry on when someone leaves; salaries or the firm's name could also be written in.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three features of a company.
questions.solution_md: Any three features, each with a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Separate legal entity: it owns property and can sue in its own name.
2. Perpetual succession: it continues despite the death or exit of members.
3. Limited liability: a shareholder answers only up to the unpaid amount on his shares.
Other features include control by a board of directors and formation by registration.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three merits of a cooperative society.
questions.solution_md: Any three merits with a line each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Equal voting rights: each member has one vote, so control is democratic.
2. Limited liability: members risk only their contribution.
3. Stable existence: registration gives it a separate legal identity, so it is not affected by changes in membership. State support and easy formation are additional merits.

questions.stem_md: State any three limitations of a Joint Hindu Family business.
questions.solution_md: Any three limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Limited capital: the family's own funds restrict growth.
2. Unlimited liability of the Karta, who may lose personal property if the business fails.
3. Dominance of the Karta: he controls decisions, and his mistakes or conflict with other members may harm the business. Managerial ability may also be limited to the family.

questions.stem_md: Anjum Siddiqui runs an imagined one-woman event-decoration business in Bhopal. Explain three limitations of this form that she may face.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations applied to Anjum's business.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Limited resources: she cannot buy costly equipment from her own savings and loans.
2. Unlimited liability: if a big event leads to losses, her house and savings can be used to pay creditors.
3. Limited managerial ability: one person must handle design, purchases, accounts and sales, and may lack skill in some areas. The business is also limited in life.

questions.stem_md: Registration of a partnership firm is optional. As of 2024, state three consequences of not registering.
questions.solution_md: Any three consequences; the credibility point is practical rather than legal.

answer.model_answer_md: As of 2024, an unregistered firm cannot file a suit against a third party to enforce a right arising from a contract. A partner cannot sue the firm or other partners to enforce a right under the deed. Also, the firm cannot claim a set-off above a certain value, and it loses some credibility with banks.

marking_scheme.step: Partners cannot sue firm or one another

questions.stem_md: Explain how capital needs and liability influence the choice of a form of organisation for an imagined firm, Deccan Robotics, which expects to need heavy investment.
questions.solution_md: Capital, liability and a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: Capital: heavy investment cannot come from one person or a few partners, so a company that can raise funds from many shareholders suits it. Liability: the founders would not wish to risk their homes, so limited liability is attractive. Hence a company, rather than a sole proprietorship or partnership, is the better choice.

marking_scheme.step: Capital need and form that suits it

questions.stem_md: Explain five types of partners.
questions.solution_md: Five types, each described in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Active partner: invests capital, shares profit and takes part in running the firm.
2. Sleeping partner: invests and shares profit but does not take part in management.
3. Secret partner: shares in management and profit, but his connection with the firm is not known to the public.
4. Nominal partner: lends his name only, with no capital or share in profit, though he is liable to outsiders.
5. Partner by estoppel: not a real partner, but liable because his conduct led others to believe he was one.

questions.stem_md: Describe the stages in forming a public company, including the dated note on commencing business.
questions.solution_md: Four stages with the dated note.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Promotion: promoters find a business idea, study its feasibility, choose a name and arrange professionals and documents.
2. Incorporation: the memorandum, articles and other papers are filed with the Registrar, who issues a certificate of incorporation, and the company comes into being.
3. Capital subscription: a public company issues a prospectus and the public applies for shares.
4. Commencement of business: as of 2024 a company with share capital files a declaration, introduced in 2019; older books speak of a certificate of commencement.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five features of a cooperative society.
questions.solution_md: Any five features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Voluntary membership: anyone with a common interest may join or leave freely.
2. Legal status: registration makes it a separate legal entity with perpetual succession.
3. Limited liability: members are liable only up to their capital contribution.
4. Democratic control: every member has one vote, whatever his shareholding.
5. Service motive: the main aim is the welfare of members, so surplus is shared on fair rules, not merely taken as profit.

questions.stem_md: Explain the features of a Joint Hindu Family business, in any five points.
questions.solution_md: Any five features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Formation: it arises from the Hindu Undivided Family under Hindu law, without a separate agreement.
2. Membership: members become coparceners by birth; as of 2024, daughters are coparceners too.
3. Management: the eldest member, the Karta, controls the business.
4. Liability: the Karta's is unlimited; the coparceners' is limited to their share.
5. Continuity: the death of the Karta does not end it; the next senior member steps up.

questions.stem_md: Explain five factors that should be weighed when choosing a form of business organisation, with a short imagined example for each.
questions.solution_md: Five factors, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Cost and ease of setting up: a roadside tea stall needs only a sole proprietorship.
2. Liability: two surgeons wanting to protect their homes may prefer a limited liability form.
3. Continuity: a family wishing the business to outlive its founder may choose a company.
4. Capital: a factory needing large funds suits a public company.
5. Control: a baker who wants to decide everything alone chooses a sole proprietorship.
Nature of the business can also matter.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a private company and a public company on any five points.
questions.solution_md: Five points of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Members: private, minimum 2 and maximum 200 as of 2024; public, minimum 7 and no maximum.
2. Directors: private, minimum 2; public, minimum 3.
3. Transfer of shares: restricted in a private company; free in a public company.
4. Public subscription: a private company cannot invite the public; a public company can.
5. Name: ends with Private Limited for the first, and Limited for the second.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five merits of a sole proprietorship.
questions.solution_md: Any five merits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Quick decisions: one person decides, so there is no delay in consulting others.
2. Confidentiality: business secrets, such as recipes or prices, stay with the owner.
3. Direct incentive: all profit belongs to the owner, which motivates hard work.
4. Sense of accomplishment: success is the owner's own, giving personal satisfaction and pride.
5. Ease of formation and closure: few legal formalities, so the business can be started or wound up quickly at low cost.
